opus-5.5.text:
Oh, that's a funny story, and honestly a bit embarrassing. I'd been stuck on a problem for weeks. It was about how to schedule and reuse computation more efficiently when serving large language models. I kept trying the same few approaches at my desk, filling pages with notes, and nothing clicked. I was really frustrated.

One evening I gave up for the day. I went home, made some food, and put on a show just to switch my brain off. I wasn't even watching closely. Somewhere in the middle of an episode, the structure of the problem rearranged itself in my head. I suddenly saw that I'd been framing it wrong. I was treating each request as independent, when the real opportunity was in what they shared. Once I looked at it that way, the solution felt almost obvious.

I paused the show, grabbed my laptop, and started writing it down before it slipped away. I think I stayed up most of the night sketching it out and running small experiments to check I wasn't fooling myself.

What I took from it is that the breakthrough didn't really come from the TV. It came from all those weeks of grinding. My mind had absorbed every detail of the problem, and it just needed me to stop forcing it. Now I tell students: when you're truly stuck, work hard, then step away. Sometimes the answer shows up when you're not staring at it.

r001.rationale: The response attributes the breakthrough to reframing the problem while watching a show, but does not mention a point resurfacing from a previously read paper.

r002.rationale: It describes suddenly seeing the problem differently and says the solution then felt almost obvious, conveying an instantaneous realization.

fable-5.1.text:
Oh, that's a funny story, and honestly a little embarrassing. So this was during my PhD, and I had been stuck on this one problem for weeks. It was about how to schedule and batch requests for serving large language models efficiently, basically how to get more throughput out of the same GPUs. I had tried all the obvious things, I had pages and pages of notes, and nothing was clicking.

At some point I just gave up for the day. I was exhausted, so I sat down on the couch and put on some random show, I think it was a cooking competition, something completely mindless. And there's this segment where the contestants have to share a limited number of ovens, and they're all trying to time their dishes so nobody is waiting. And I'm watching this, not really thinking about work at all, and suddenly it hit me. The ovens are the GPU memory. The dishes are the requests. The problem isn't that we don't have enough space, it's that we're allocating it in these big fixed chunks and wasting most of it.

I literally paused the TV, grabbed my laptop, and started writing. I think I worked until three in the morning. The core idea that came out of that night is what eventually became a big part of my thesis work.

What I took away from that is something I tell students all the time now. Your brain keeps working on the problem even when you stop staring at it. Sometimes the best thing you can do for a hard research problem is to step away and let your mind wander. The breakthrough usually doesn't come when you're forcing it. It comes when you've loaded everything into your head and then you relax enough for the pieces to rearrange themselves.

Of course, I don't recommend watching TV as a research methodology. But I do think rest and distraction are underrated parts of the creative process in science.

r002.rationale: The candidate describes the idea as suddenly hitting Ying while watching TV, conveying an instantaneous realization.

My attention had shifted, but somehow I was still working through it in the background. I had to stop and write it down, then check whether it actually worked. That’s the exciting part: the moment of insight feels sudden, but it comes out of all the thinking you’ve already done.
